analysis.one_liner: Tightens Medicare Advantage and drug plan marketing rules, creates a complaint system, and gives seniors more time to switch plans.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe with four cosponsors from the other parties, never received a committee vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a formal system for tracking complaints from seniors about their private Medicare Advantage and prescription drug plans, made those complaints public, and required insurers to fix patterns of problems. It would have banned hard-sell marketing tactics — free meals, cold calls, and pitching extra products to people signing up for Medicare plans. It also would have let seniors back out of a new plan within 60 days and given them more time each fall to compare and switch plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plans. They would get an accessible, public complaint-tracking system run through the Medicare Beneficiary Ombudsman, a ban on inducements like meals and on telemarketing, cross-selling, and up-selling, disclosure of which doctors refuse to see enrollees in certain private plans, the right to leave a new plan within 60 days, a longer annual window to switch plans, and coordinated enrollment rules for drug plans [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to build a plan complaint system that logs every complaint from Medicare Advantage and Part D enrollees, tracks it through resolution, investigates whether complaints reflect a pattern, and makes complaint information available to the public [S2][S3].

It prohibits Medicare Advantage organizations and prescription drug plan sponsors from offering meals or items of monetary value to induce enrollment, and from marketing by telemarketing, in-home solicitation, cross-selling of non-Medicare products, or up-selling from drug plans to Medicare Advantage plans — unless the senior requested it [S2][S3].

Non-network Medicare Advantage private fee-for-service plans would have to disclose which providers in their service area refused to accept plan enrollees in the past 12 months, so seniors would know before enrolling whether their own doctor would take the plan [S2][S3].

It lets a person discontinue enrollment in a Medicare plan if enrolled fewer than 60 days, moves the annual coordinated election period start from November 15 to October 1 to give more comparison time, and coordinates Part D drug plan enrollment rules with the Medicare plan rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage organizations and prescription drug plan sponsors, who would bear the cost of restricting their sales practices, tracking and responding to logged complaints, and publishing provider-refusal lists. Taxpayers would fund the complaint system, since the bill authorizes appropriations of such sums as may be necessary for it [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private Medicare and drug plan insurers

drawbacks.text: The complaint system is funded with an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as may be necessary,' with no cost estimate or spending cap attached, leaving the price to taxpayers unquantified [S3].

The marketing bans would restrict not only high-pressure tactics but also ordinary cross-selling and up-selling, which insurers could argue limits their ability to tell enrollees about products or plan options that might help them — the bill's carve-out applies only when the senior specifically asks [S3].

The requirement to publish lists of providers who refused private fee-for-service enrollees could stigmatize doctors whose refusal reflected disputes over plan payment rates rather than any judgment about patients [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are aimed at a real problem: seniors were signing up for private plans through aggressive sales tactics and had no systematic way to flag bad actors. The complaint-tracking and disclosure provisions are modest in cost and straightforward in design. The main honest trade-offs are the uncapped federal cost of the complaint system and the fact that some of the marketing restrictions go beyond banning pressure tactics to limiting ordinary sales conversations. On balance the bill offered clear protections to seniors at a limited, largely administrative cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on March 3, 2008, for herself and Sen. John Rockefeller, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S3][S5].
Four senators cosponsored the bill: three Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The committee took no further action — the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers and prescription drug plan sponsors, who avoided the marketing restrictions, complaint tracking, and provider disclosure requirements; seniors gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 3, 2008 and took no action — no markup, no committee vote, no report — for the remaining ten months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator led the bill, joined by three Democratic and one Independent cosponsors; there were no recorded votes to show how the parties would have lined up on passage.

industries.note: The bill bans inducements like meals, telemarketing, cross-selling, and up-selling, requires disclosure of doctors who refuse plan enrollees, lets seniors exit within 60 days, and feeds every complaint into a public tracking system. Each provision constrains sales practices and increases scrutiny of plans whose revenue comes from Medicare enrollment decisions seniors make.

The same marketing prohibitions would apply directly to drug plan sponsors, and enrollment and disenrollment rules would be coordinated with the Medicare plan rules, reducing sponsors' control over when and how seniors join or leave their plans.

industries.industry: Health insurance sales and marketing firms
industries.note: Cold-calling, in-home solicitation, and cross-selling non-Medicare products to Medicare enrollees are the core business practices this bill prohibits, eliminating those sales channels unless the senior initiates contact.

industries.industry: Physicians treating private fee-for-service plan enrollees
industries.note: Doctors keep their freedom to refuse enrollees of private fee-for-service plans, but any refusal in the previous 12 months would be published on a plan-by-plan list, adding public pressure without changing payment disputes.
